patterns_found.visual_evidence: The desktop sketch shows a distinct top header/navigation area separated by a horizontal rule above the main article content, suggesting a persistent masthead that remains available while reading a long page.
patterns_found.behavior_notes: Header/navigation should likely stay fixed or become fixed on scroll so branding/navigation remains accessible during long-form reading.
patterns_found.ambiguities: The sketch does not explicitly show a scrolled state, so stickiness is inferred from the long article layout rather than directly drawn.

patterns_found.visual_evidence: The desktop sketch includes a compact header area with small utility-like items near the top, consistent with a blog header that commonly contains search access.
patterns_found.behavior_notes: If implemented, search should support focus, text entry, and submit behavior; it may expand from a compact trigger in the header.
patterns_found.ambiguities: The sketch marks are abstract and do not clearly label a search field, so this is only weakly implied by the header utility layout and reference structure.

patterns_found.visual_evidence: The desktop article layout includes a large featured image block within a blog post; large editorial images commonly imply click-to-open enlarged viewing or sharing/subscription overlays in this kind of design.
patterns_found.behavior_notes: If images or utility actions are interactive, a modal/lightbox overlay would open above the page, trap focus, and close via close button, Escape, or backdrop.
patterns_found.ambiguities: The sketch does not explicitly depict an overlay trigger or modal state; this is inferred from the prominent image treatment and common blog behavior.

patterns_found.visual_evidence: Near the lower portion of the desktop sketch there is a boxed input-like area beneath divider lines, consistent with a comment or subscription form region.
patterns_found.behavior_notes: Any comment/subscription form should validate required fields before submission and surface inline errors or submission status.
patterns_found.ambiguities: The exact form type and fields are not labeled, so validation requirements are inferred from the presence of an input region rather than explicit controls.

patterns_found.visual_evidence: Both sketches depict long vertically stacked content areas typical of blog/article feeds or extended comment/content sections, implying progressive disclosure or pagination behavior may be needed to avoid rendering everything at once.
patterns_found.behavior_notes: A load-more trigger could append additional posts, comments, or related items below the visible content while preserving reading position.
patterns_found.ambiguities: The sketches do not show a labeled button or spinner, so this is speculative and depends on whether the page is a single post view or a feed.

patterns_found.visual_evidence: Any interactive overlays, search activation, or form regions implied by the layouts would require managed keyboard focus; the desktop especially suggests header utilities and a lower-page form area, while the mobile long reading layout would need orderly focus progression.
patterns_found.behavior_notes: Programmatic focus should move into opened overlays or expanded search, return to the trigger on close, and maintain logical tab order through long-form content.
patterns_found.ambiguities: This pattern is dependent on the presence of other interactive components, some of which are only implied rather than explicitly drawn.

sketch_notes: The sketches imply a mostly content-first blog/article experience with relatively light but important JavaScript needs rather than a highly app-like interface. Desktop suggests more utility behavior in the header and lower-page interaction around forms, while mobile appears primarily as a long reading view with minimal explicit controls. Most complexity comes from inferred enhancements common to editorial/blog layouts—sticky header behavior, possible search activation, possible image/modal treatment, and accessible focus handling—rather than clearly drawn widgets like tabs, accordions, or menus.
